extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners applying MPEP eligibility guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims under the Alice/Mayo subject-matter eligibility framework (Steps 2A and 2B), focusing on whether claims are directed to abstract ideas or to an improvement in computer-related technology or other technology. Includes categories of judicially-identified abstract ideas and non-limiting examples of eligible and ineligible claim types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and claim must reflect an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement, and the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should assess whether the specification and claims show an improvement to computer-functionality or other technology (see MPEP § 2106.05(a)). If the disclosure and claim language do not reflect an improvement, eligibility is less likely. Examples and case law are cited to help determine whether claimed subject matter improves technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope must be a particular solution, not merely an idea/outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the extent to which the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome, as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim ties the abstract idea to a specific technical implementation or merely preempts an idea. Also consider whether the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) limits the claim to computer implementation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for discussion and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims performable without a computer are not improvements in computer technology
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed process can be performed without a computer, the Federal Circuit has indicated that it cannot be characterized as an improvement in a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Synopsys, Inc. v. Mentor Graphics Corp. (839 F.3d 1138) — method that could be performed mentally or without a computer was not an improvement in computer technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere automation or speed-up by a general-purpose computer is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere automation of manual processes or increasing the speed of a process where these purported improvements come solely from the capabilities of a general-purpose computer are not sufficient to show an improvement in computer-functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See FairWarning IP, LLC v. Iatric Sys. and Credit Acceptance Corp. v. Westlake Services for Federal Circuit guidance that generic computer implementation that only automates or speeds up is inadequate to establish an improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: More than conventional implementation on generic components required
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must include more than conventional implementation on generic components or machinery to qualify as an improvement to an existing technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that add only well-known computer components or conventional machinery likely fail to show improved computer-functionality (see Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications v. AV Auto.). Examiners should look for unconventional arrangement or operation that improves technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve improvement question as early as possible (Step 2A or 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the question of whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology may be considered in either step of the Alice/Mayo test (Step 2A or 2B), examiners are encouraged to resolve this question as early as possible in the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an improvement is clear, eligibility may be resolved under a streamlined analysis (Pathway A) or found not directed to an abstract idea (Pathway B). If improvement is not clear, it still may contribute to eligibility under Step 2B. See discussion referencing Enfish and Amdocs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement can render claim eligible at Step 2A or contribute at Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is directed to a clear improvement in computer-related technology may be eligible at Pathway A under the streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea; if improvement is less clear it may still contribute to eligibility in the Step 2B analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Enfish claims (self-referential table) found eligible as improvement; Amdocs claims (distributed network architecture) were eligible under Step 2B because the unconventional architecture amounted to an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must recite an abstract idea to be directed to it (Step 2A principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Step 2A analysis requires a claim to recite (i.e., set forth or describe) an abstract idea in order to be directed to that idea. Claims that are based on or involve an abstract idea but do not recite it are not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle separates claims that merely use or involve abstract ideas from claims that are actually directed to those ideas. See Enfish, DDR Holdings, Trading Techs. examples and the non-limiting hypothetical examples (printer, washing machine, earring sensor, BRCA sequencing, BIOS loading) that illustrate claims not reciting an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim recites abstract idea but claim as whole is an improvement, it is not directed to abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claims reciting an abstract idea are not directed to the abstract idea because they also recite additional elements (such as an improvement) demonstrating that the claims as a whole clearly do not seek to tie up the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found that additional elements which improve computer functioning or other technology shift the focus from the abstract idea (see McRO; Enfish; Research Corporation Technologies). Non-limiting examples include surgical shears with a pressure regulator, robotic arm with sensor-based control, autofocus camera system, and an internal combustion engine with a control system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on concepts identified in cases, not the judicial descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claimed concept is similar to a concept the courts have identified as an abstract idea, examiners should rely on the concepts identified in the cases, not the judicial descriptors themselves (e.g., 'fundamental economic practices').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptors are not mutually exclusive and can overlap; use the factual and conceptual holdings of precedent to assess similarity (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) discussion and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: 'Fundamental economic practices' as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to the economy and commerce, such as agreements between people, financial transactions, pricing, and hedging, are examples of concepts the courts have described as 'fundamental economic practices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples include buySAFE (transaction guaranty), OIP Technologies (price testing/pricing optimization), Bilski (hedging). Other examples: processing financing applications, wagering rules. Use these case concepts to compare claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Concepts relating to mitigating risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts directed to mitigating risks (e.g., intermediated settlement to mitigate settlement risk) have been identified as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank characterized intermediated settlement as an abstract idea. Compare claimed risk-mitigation schemes to the concepts in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Certain methods of organizing human activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to interpersonal and intrapersonal activities—managing relationships or transactions between people, social activities, satisfying or avoiding legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales, and managing human mental activity—have been described as 'methods of organizing human activity' and can be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all organization-of-human-activity claims are abstract; the qualifier 'certain' is a reminder. Case examples: buySAFE, Dealertrack (credit application processing), Bancorp (insurance policy management). Analyze whether claimed steps merely implement such organization or provide a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategory: Advertising, marketing, and sales activities as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to advertising, marketing, and sales activities (e.g., generating/transmitting menus, structuring a sales force, using advertising as exchange) can be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Apple v. Ameranth (menu generation), In re Ferguson (structuring sales force), Ultramercial (advertising as currency). Claims that simply add conventional computer components to these business practices are likely abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategory: Managing human behavior as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that implement schemes to influence or track human behavior (e.g., budgeting notifications, filtering content, diagnostic mental processes) can be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One (tracking spending limits), BASCOM (content filtering treated as abstract under Step 2A), In re Meyer (mental process). Assess whether claim adds a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategory: Tracking or organizing information as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to tracking, organizing, or manipulating information (e.g., data filtering, particular GUI arrangements to improve accuracy) may be abstract ideas depending on whether they provide a technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BASCOM (content filtering) and Trading Techs. (GUI display improving trader accuracy) provide examples where the concept was considered; examine whether the claim recites a specific technical solution that improves computer operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting examples of claims that do not recite an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include: a printer comprising a belt, roller, printhead, ink cartridge; a washing machine with drive motor and controller; an earring with a blood-glucose sensor and memory; method for sequencing BRCA1; method for loading BIOS into a local computer system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate claims that do not set forth or describe an abstract idea. Use such concrete device or method examples to distinguish from claims that recite abstract concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting examples of claims not directed to an abstract idea because of an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include: surgical shears with a pressure regulator limiting applied force; a robotic arm assembly with sensor-based velocity adjustment for smooth motion; autofocus camera system combining autofocus algorithm and drive mechanism; an internal combustion engine with EGR valve controlled by processor based on throttle rate of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These show claims where additional elements clearly improved the functioning of the claimed technology and therefore were not directed to an abstract idea. Examiners should identify analogous technical improvements in examined claims.
